articles.author: Julianne Malveaux, PhD
articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. In his run-up to the midterm elections, the president is crisscrossing the country in an effort to energize his base. Unfortunately, he seeks to inflame his base with multiple exaggerations, obfuscations, half-truths, and downright bald-faced lies. Thus, he told Oklahoma’s News 9 on October 1, “So we have the greatest economy in the history of our country.” The data says otherwise. Consider the September employment report, released October 2. The economy added just 29,000 jobs. Earlier estimates for July and August were revised downward by a combined 60,000. articles.author: Marcus Baram
articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Almost no one ran on climate change this fall, but the election may reshape climate policy all the same. articles.title: Los Angeles Socialists Won Big in the Blue Electoral Wave
articles.author: Chris Kutalik
articles.content_excerpt: LA was at a critical cusp in its history. Globalization had reorganized its economy, rewiring it in dramatic ways, and many people were being left behind. Yet the city had — and still has — this incredible, protean potential for better things, for progressive politics, for surprising activism. — Mike Davis, 2006 The midterm elections were truly seismic. Like many places across the country, Los Angeles made good on its protean potential from the 2026 blowout with a stronger socialist movement and a larger share of political power. Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) members won up and down the ballot. Nithya Raman won the mayor’s office of the country’s second-largest city in an upset victory. articles.title: The Enshittification of Everyday Life
articles.author: Jatinder Hayre
articles.content_excerpt: Have you tried to speak to a human being lately? Perhaps you wanted to question an energy bill, rearrange a hospital appointment, claim a benefit, or discover why your insurer had refused treatment your doctor said you needed. You will probably have been invited to download an app, create an account, and remember a password. The most recent demand is that you must interrogate a chatbot. And then, as a final act of administrative penance, you can telephone a call center, where a recorded voice assures you that your call is terribly important. Somewhere along the way, a strange inversion occurred: the institution still takes your money, increasingly so, but you perform more and more of the labor. articles.title: What the ’60s Left Gave Us
articles.author: Adolph Reed
articles.content_excerpt: Before the Bernie Sanders presidential runs, the last big upsurge in radical American politics occurred in the 1960s. This moment is remembered for its civil rights activism and student antiwar protests, but how should we really understand the New Left’s rise and fall? On this latest episode of the Jacobin Radio podcast Confronting Capitalism , Vivek Chibber and Melissa Naschek are joined by political scientist and longtime socialist organizer Adolph Reed Jr for a wide-ranging conversation about the ’60s radicals. They look at the rise of the student movement, the developments in postwar Marxism, and the birth of modern identity politics. articles.author: Socialist Forum
articles.content_excerpt: American politics is at a crossroads. All that was once considered certain or possible is now in question. For the first time since the early 20th century, American Socialists are gaining considerable municipal and state level influence through successful and highly publicized electoral campaigns. After a largely successful midterm showing, the DSA established itself as a small but potent force in American politics. For the first time there is a comparatively large cohort of elected DSA members holding local, state, and federal office. Along with this heightened political influence comes greater political risk. articles.title: David Dinkins Wasn’t Loud Enough for New York City
articles.author: David Duhalde
articles.content_excerpt: In the past few weeks, New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani has proposed breaking up the Strategic Response Group and closing Rikers by 2032 , the former established by progressive Mayor Bill de Blasio, who also revived a plan to dismantle the latter by 2027. But unfulfilled promises of police and carceral reform efforts go back to the 1990s. How much should the failures of previous mayoral administrations weigh on the decisions of Mamdani and his allies in regard to public safety and police? This question has no easy answer.
